subsubtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL-ESCAPE OF FIVE INMATES-ALLEGED WARNING OF ATTEMPT TO ESCAPE-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
My question, Mr. Speaker, is directed to the Solicitor General and arises out of the reply given in this chamber yesterday by the minister when I asked him about the escape of five extremely dangerous inmates from Laval security institution. The minister said at that time:
I might say that we had put out special orders in respect of these men some time ago ... For some reason or other these orders I had given, and which had been given by the Commissioner of Penitentiaries, were not followed.
Can the Solicitor General advise us whether these special instructions concerning these extremely dangerous inmates were given by him, because as far back as three weeks ago the minister and his officials had been warned by the Quebec provincial police that these inmates, three of whom had already previously escaped, would make another attempt to do so?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL-ESCAPE OF FIVE INMATES-ALLEGED WARNING OF ATTEMPT TO ESCAPE-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was never advised by the Quebec provincial police, nor was the Commissioner of Penitentiaries. When I heard yesterday that the Quebec provincial police had advised somebody in the service, I immediately checked to find out who in the Quebec provincial police advised the penitentiary service, and I want to know whom they advised. I only found that out yesterday afternoon. I am waiting for a report on that particular point. If in fact the Quebec provincial police did advise our officials, and it seems they did, this means that there is even more negligence on the part of someone in the system, but I was not advised, and the people in Ottawa were not advised.

subsubtopic: ST. VINCENT DE PAUL-ESCAPE OF FIVE INMATES-ALLEGED WARNING OF ATTEMPT TO ESCAPE-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a supplementary to the minister who speaks about negligence in the system. The minister has now admitted that the Quebec provincial police some three weeks ago warned that this escape would be attempted. The minister now admits he was not advised by his officials.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is distorting what I said and also what he has been reading in the press. I said that I have been advised that the Quebec provincial police advised people in my department that there would be an escape. I checked into that. I want to know who gave the advice and who received the advice. I did not get that advice and the Commissioner of Penitentiaries did not get it. On the other point, Mr. Speaker, as with many things that happen I am waiting for a report on the whole issue before I accuse any particular individual of negligence. It seems to me there is negligence somewhere. There has to be when you have such flagrant violations of the ordinary regulations. We will get a report, Mr. Speaker, and then action will be taken.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE IN NUMBER OF MEAT INSPECTORS- POSSIBILITY OF MORE SEVERE PENALTIES FOR OFFENCES AGAINST REGULATIONS CONCERNING MEAT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. As I told him yesterday, I have given instructions to increase the inspection and improve the standards. I expect regulations to be promulgated to improve standards in the very near future. This will be the result of consultations that have already taken place with private industry and the various departments of the government. At the present time, over 245 people are assigned to food programs in the Field Operation Directorate of my department. I have given instructions to immediately assign 30 of these people in the field to work exclusively on meat samples across the country. This would be in addition to the 1,255 meat inspectors of the Department of Agriculture and the 195 inspectors in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs involved in various aspects of food inspection. It should also be noted that provincial and municipal governments also have inspectors who are involved in food inspection. This has all to be kept in perspective. Canada has a food inspection program that compares favourably with any other country and I intend to keep it that way.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel the House should forget about carcasses and proceed to live cattle.
I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture. The minister is certainly aware of the extremely disastrous situation resulting from the fact that cattle producers are being offered for their production prices which amount to 25 per cent of their costs. Does the minister consider this matter as urgent and does he intend to introduce measures shortly to help these producers cope with their difficulties?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: BEEF CATTLE-REQUEST FOR AID TO PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I said earlier this week we are considering doing something. The hon. member must be patient for a little longer. There are five provinces which now have programs. These are based on the federal stabilization program to assist the beef raisers in those provinces which have made the announcements. The programs are based on

our stabilization program under which we guarantee 90 per cent of production costs over a five-year period. We are still being asked by the provinces to share in the programs they have initiated. Some of these programs are very different. It is very difficult to work out a cost sharing arrangement for some of the programs they have said they are going to use and, in fact, have put into force for the people in their provinces. We are trying to work out something for Canadian beef producers that will coincide with what the provinces are doing.

subsubtopic: BEEF CATTLE-REQUEST FOR AID TO PRODUCERS

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: BEEF CATTLE-REQUEST FOR AID TO PRODUCERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the main concerns is that we must keep the production. If we lose that, it will cost the consumers much more in the months and years ahead. It takes four years to get back into beef production once you get out of it. We are all concerned about that. Some of the provincial programs are very good. The program which the province of Quebec has put in to supplement the beef stabilization program compares with that of any other province. If the hon. member will study the situation, he will see that it is one of the best initiated by any province. That does not mean we are not going to do anything. We will be making a proposal next week.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs a question but before doing so may I personally thank him for interviewing Mr. Fieger of Calgary regarding the situation in Mexico. speechtext:

With regard to the alleged maltreatment of Mr. Fieger in a Mexican jail, we brought this allegation to the attention of the Mexican authorities and at our request an investigation was held. It was reported that there was no evidence of maltreatment.
I did meet Mr. Fieger in September, I believe, and at that time I read a letter that his son had sent to his father whom I met. At that time, as I recollect, the letter stated

that there was no evidence of maltreatment as attested to by the inmate himself. As for the other points, I will get the information and provide it to the hon. member.

subtopic: INCARCERATION OF MR. FIEGER IN MEXICO-ALLEGATIONS OF BRUTALITY-REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I put a further question to the minister. I have a copy of the letter he refers to, but the alleged brutality took place before the report was made to the former minister of external affairs. The minister says there was an investigation, but the investigation was conducted by Mexican authorities, not Canadian authorities. The right hon. member for Prince Albert also asked the minister about this matter, and in view of the conflict between the Mexican authorities, and in view of the fact that mail has to be smuggled out of the jail-the inmates pay for their own keep or they do not eat-would the minister agree that an independent group of Canadians should be allowed to investigate the whole matter? According to the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights, whatever the facts are, if a Canadian is incarcerated in the jail of another country he should be treated with the same kind of dignity we would treat other citizens who found themselves in the same situation in Canada.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INCARCERATION OF MR. FIEGER IN MEXICO-ALLEGATIONS OF BRUTALITY-REQUEST FOR INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the standard that has to be applied, presumably in all institutions, is that inmates, regardless of origin, should be treated alike. It would not be possible for us to implant into another country practices that we have in this country. The suggestion that we have an independent inquiry into conditions in Mexican jails in order to satisfy ourselves would probably be resisted by any independent sovereign nation, including Canada if another country suggested the same thing. I hesitate to propose a policy or practice that would, by its very nature, be bound to fail.

I should like to know if the statement of the Indian land claims commissioner means there are to be new government initiatives in the area of aboriginal rights.

Mr. Chairman, let me begin by offering congratulations to the minister on the assumption of his responsibilities. I think it is agreed he has made an encouraging start in his portfolio, and it is well known that he comes to the department with a background of goodwill among its constituents. I want to point out to him, however, that while he has goodwill in the three areas of his responsibility, it is also a very clear fact that the mandate won by his government was denied him in each of the three areas of the north where the election returned members of this party and the New Democratic Party to represent the native people of Canada and certainly those within the national parks. I hope he will bear that fact in mind if there is ever temptation to carry too far the idea of upgrading the government's mandate as a result of the July election. I think the minister clearly has a special responsibility in that he is the first new minister to hold this portfolio for a long time. Many members of this House, and people who have to deal with the department, hope he will take advantage of his status as a new minister to change some of the people and some of the procedures that clearly were not working well in dealing with the problems of the native people and the northern territories. There has been no approval of the status quo as it relates to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. We hope the minister is aware of this as he assumes his responsibilities.
Mr. Chairman, I want to begin by referring to the statement made many times and repeated in the standing committee by the president of the National Indian Brotherhood, George Manuel, who expressed concern about the bureaucracy with which the native people have to deal. I recognize that the minister claimed last night that the bureaucratic proportion of his department amounts to only 7 per cent. I am not interested in arguing percentages, but I am interested in ensuring that the public servants involved in the administration of this department are helping to achieve the goals of native people, national parks and northern policy, and are not serving as obstructionists. I think it is recognized that it is the view of the National Indian Brotherhood that in many cases these public servants are obstructive.
I wonder, in view of the opinion recently articulated by the new parliamentary secretary to the minister, whether we may look forward to the day when the department will phase itself out, whether there is any concrete plan to reduce the number of public service employees in the
Estimates
department or the proportion of the budget that goes to administration costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. member for the kind remarks that he made prior to bringing me down to earth with a thud through his caution. I do not accept the idea that people employed in this department serve as obstructionists. By and large, a great many dedicated people are employed in all aspects of the operation of the department. There is no question that there is a transition in progress in the role of many employees and administrators and managers are being moved more into the role of advisers as the programs are being taken on and administered by the Indian people.
I indicated last evening that roughly $60 million of the budget is now handled directly by the band councils and Indian associations. I think this is the basic thrust, and the role is changing. As I said last evening, the number of employees in the department who are concerned with Indian and Eskimo Affairs programs has remained static for the last half-dozen years, but the budget has gone up threefold. So there has been a substantial increase in the funds used on behalf of the clientele of this department.
Let me repeat my specific question. Does the department or the minister intend, over a stated period of time, say five or ten years, to wind down the department? Is there any such plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: No, there is not. The hon. member may recall that in 1969 the federal government put out a policy statement dealing with Indian and Eskimo Affairs programs. This policy was put out for consideration. One of its proposals was precisely in line with the hon. member's suggestion. With few exceptions, there was strong reaction on the part of the Indian people against acceptance of the proposals in that document. The Prime Minister and my predecessor undertook, to a group of Indian people who came to a meeting, that the government would not unilaterally make the suggested changes. Again, I should mention that this proposed revision is now being conducted with regard to the Indian Act. We hope at some time in future to straighten this out and move ahead. But that undertaking was given.

Mr. Chairman, the minister knows as well as I do that the objection of the Indian people in this country was not related so much to the contents of that report as to the means by which the report was put together. It was done by virtually ignoring the undertaking given by the minister's predecessor to consult with the Indian people.
I do not want to rake over old coals, but the matter of consultation is one to which I shall return. Let me remind the minister of the repeated request of the president of the National Indian Brotherhood. That organization seeks a complete and detailed review of the structure and operation of the Indian and Eskimo Affairs branch of the department. Will the minister accede to that request and allow the National Indian Brotherhood unfettered access to the records of the department so that a complete and full review can be undertaken by the National Indian Brotherhood? In that way we shall allay the apprehension

Estimates
of the Indian people that the bureaucracy of the department is working against them. Will the minister give us that commitment? Will he say yes or no, because time is short.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I said last evening, a consultative mechanism was set up for discussions with the National Indian Brotherhood. If they make such a precise request at their next meeting in Feburary with the cabinet committee, I will be prepared to take a serious look at it.

In other words, we have the commitment that when George Manuel repeats his specific request for a full, detailed and unfettered review of the operations of Indian and Eskimo Affairs programs, the minister may not accede to that request but he will give serious consideration to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, yes, more or less. The point is that George Manuel does not set the agenda. The executive of the National Indian Brotherhood does. If the National Indian Brotherhood wants to give that item top priority, it will be considered.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that it may be less, not more. Let me point out that this kind of double-talk, this refusal to accede to the request of the democratically elected representatives of the Indian people of Canada, creates suspicion and difficulty among these people who deal with the department. Turning specifically to the question of consultation-

speechtext: Order please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member. I remind him that the time allotted to him under the agreed ten-minute limitation of speeches has now expired.

Mr. Chairman, I was very glad yesterday to note the great objectives that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) announced concerning the policies of his department. I was somewhat surprised after listening to the speech of the minister to hear some people come back and say that we should try to involve the Indians and the Inuits in the fields of education, housing and cultural affairs, since the minister had just told us that the main objective of his department was to give as much autonomy, freedom and independence as possible to the Indians as concerns the administration of their own affairs.
It is obvious, Mr. Chairman, since education concerns me particularly, that this is a field where the independence of individuals is extremely important. Indeed, the very aim of education is to achieve an independent status as an individual. However, education itself involves a contradiction since education also means training and training nearly always implies certain restrictions. Several years ago, we acted restrictively towards the Indians because we wanted to mold them or bring them to see things our way and to share our cultural, linguistic and other values.
I am very glad, Mr. Chairman, to see that the objective of the department is to give back to our native people, the

Indians and the Inuits, through a grant of a few million dollars, the means to regain their own linguistic, cultural and educational independence.
Yesterday some comments referred to the number of Indians who take part in their own education, either by being teachers or in some other way. It is quite obvious that the restrictive action taken in the past has eliminated some native people from this process of education, particularly in the field of teaching.
If one looks at the progress made and characterized by statistics provided by the minister, one sees the movement is going in a positive way and towards ever increasing native involvement in that process at all levels.
I am quite happy to see that the votes allocated to the cultural and educational areas follow precisely that objective of involvement, and I am convinced that in a few years the minister's statistics will be higher. We will then see that for the larger part, Indians will be looking after their education, their other problems and dealing with them themselves.
I would like to point out another thing, Mr. Chairman, about the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development with respect to Parks Canada. I think the minister went over an aspect of Parks Canada much too quickly yesterday and I am referring to the byways and historic sites. I find that program particularly interesting because a few years ago there was talk already that that program about byways and historic travel routes would help link the core of Ontario to Quebec City.
Mr. Chairman, that route would go through the whole riding of Portneuf where the sites are magnificent, the scenery beautiful and one could also find famous historic sites such as the old Jacques-Cartier Fort at Donnacona. That panoramic route on those byways would make it possible for the people of Quebec City to admire the beautiful scenery in a natural environment. That would also allow us to preserve our natural resources in their state of wilderness.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister intends to make a greater effort to have this special route built. I would also like to know whether the minister is still consulting with Ontario and Quebec so that those magnificent projects are achieved as soon as possible.
Mr. Chairman, in conclusion, I want to express to the minister my best wishes for success in his new duties. I am very happy to see that on this side of the House there are a great many people as dynamic and intelligent as the minister who can be called upon to continue the good work of those who leave their posts.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to reply briefly to the hon. member for Portneuf, I share his concern as far as the parks and sites aspect is concerned. In fact, when I was making some remarks last evening I think the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre sort of jokingly asked what I meant by the term "linear parks". I think this program is becoming more and more effective in parts of our country which are heavily populated, such as the Windsor-Quebec City access. It is going to be more dif-
October 25, 1974

ficult to put together the large land assemblies we will need to create this type of park. We will have to look at other types of programs such as by-ways and canals to try to create ways for Canadians in heavily populated areas to gain some meaningful experience from our parks system.
How about the Grand River?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Perhaps the Grand River as well, and your 66-foot footpath. For a good many people, even in our national parks such as Banff and Jasper the experience is pretty well limited to the road, interpretation centre and the visitors' centre. I think you can make a very strong case that canals, and so on, are areas to which we should be devoting a significant amount of attention.
I wish to report that nothing has been concluded; we are still very much in the negotiation stage. One of my first acts was to go, with Hon. Allan Grossman who has responsibility for this area in Ontario, to look at the Blueridge parkway in the United States to see whether it had any application for Canada. I wish to reassure the hon. member that while I cannot report anything substantive at this time, we are still very interested in a Laurentian parkway from Quebec City to the province of Ontario.

Mr. Chairman, I join other members in congratulating the minister upon his ascension to this important and interesting portfolio. Unfortunately, he has arrived at this position when many of the long-standing problems have reached crisis proportions.
I was interested in the presentation of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands and the statement of the Indian land claims commissioner who until recent times has been a fairly moderate and mild man with regard to land claims. He is now reaching the point where he is becoming strongly critical.
Because of the shortage of time, I wish to zero in immediately on the subject I have in mind. In a recent interview with Joan Cohen, as reported in the October 15 issue of the Ottawa Citizen, Harold Cardinal made some pointed remarks on the deterioration of the Indian situation across Canada. Included in this article was the following interesting statement:
And as serious as anything, the announced reform of the education system, which was to have put schools under the control of Indians, simply didn't materialize. The Department of Indian Affairs is running things, just as it always did.
That is why he sees it as essential that economic and education reforms be separated from the long-term policy decisions that have to be made when discussions begin with the federal government.
I think the minister is much more sensitive on these matters because he has been chairman of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and has gone through the inevitable educational process of chairing that group of MPs. However, as recently as last week the National Indian Brotherhood made a statement which has been made repeatedly, that the white man speaks with a forked tongue. There is some justification for this with respect to education. We had a formal, staged press conference held on May 24, 1973, where the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the president of the National Indian Brotherhood, George Manuel, announced the implementation of the new look in education which had been derived from the committee's report
Estimates
of June, 1971, and the Indian Brotherhood statement on Indian culture and education which was released, I believe, in 1972. On that occasion, the minister made this commitment, and I quote from his official statement:
I have given the National Indian Brotherhood my assurance that I and my department are fully committed to realizing the educational goals for the Indian people which are set forth in the Brotherhood's proposal. In consultation and co-operation with the Indian organizations, my department will begin immediately to effect the educational changes for the Indian people that they have requested.
Obviously, this undertaking has not been discharged, if we are to accept the words of Harold Cardinal who has been a very responsible and discerning leader in matters affecting our Canadian Indians. I want to ask specific questions to see if we can get any information as to how far this program has gone. We might not have time to get all the answers. If the minister is not able to deal with them in the chamber this afternoon, perhaps he will send me written answers.
In order to implement the program, as Mr. Cardinal says, priorities must be given to economic and educational matters. I agree with that statement. As H. G. Wells said, civilization is a race between education and catastrophe. I think we can translate that into the critical situation facing our native people at the present time. How many staff members at the upper echelon in the education branch of the Department of Indian Affairs are native people? What are their positions? This information is essential if we are to implement the objective of the Indians themselves in regaining control over education. The priorities were expressed in their paper as parental responsibility and local control.
Second, how much do the funds amount to that are available for experimental and innovative projects? How have they been used? This is one of the points made in the minister's statement of 1973. Third, how far has the process of the provincial curriculum enrichment proceeded? What provinces have taken action? How far down into the local educational level has this program proceeded? Fourth, how many native cultural educational centres have been established under this specific program? Of the $40 million that was allocated, how much has been spent, and for what specific programs?
The next question concerns an item for professional and special services, the amount of which keeps going up. I notice from the current estimates it has increased by $4.5 million to a level of $82 million. What is this particular estimate used for, what reports have been produced, how many people have been involved in those reports, and who are they? Are Indian research projects funded from this item of special services amounting to $82 million? Is there not overlapping and duplication in making available this amount of money, a substantial sum that might be more directly funnelled into the educational process itself?
I think that will suffice for the moment. If the minister would start his answer, he could then perhaps send me a written reply.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. member for his kind comments. I am more optimistic than the Indian claims commissioner regarding the
28305-4 9'/j

October 25, 1974
Estimates
matter of Indian land claims. I feel that we are reasonably close to some sort of significant breakthrough in Quebec. If that is accomplished, I think hon. members will find that a settlement there will more or less establish the parameters of claim settlements and that there will be faster movement in the Yukon, the Northwest Territories and British Columbia. I am talking now basically in the area of comprehensive claims as opposed to the specific claims being made in the treaty areas. As I say, frankly I am more optimistic than is the Indian claims commissioner in this regard.
Moving on to the hon. member's next area of questioning, the basic commitment of the government to the undertaking made by the minister and Mr. Manuel when they appeared before our committee, the government is still committed in this area. Progress has not been as rapid as we would like, partly because-the hon. member will recall this statement being made in the committee-the government could not really walk away from the joint agreements that we had entered into throughout this country with provincial school boards. This could be one of the areas of greatest difficulty.
We have incurred very substantial capital costs in buying places for Indian children in schools, and we are locked into ongoing contracts for the provision of educational services. No doubt this creates a very awkward situation; the Indian people would like to terminate these things, move out and spend very significant sums on duplicating these facilities on the reserves. The cost implications of this, as Mr. Manuel appreciated when we were discussing the matter before the committee, are very great, so that progress has not been nearly as rapid so far as getting schools established is concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I very much regret interrupting the minister, but I want to recognize another hon. member before we adjourn for lunch. Since the time for this set of questions is over, perhaps the minister could adopt the suggestion of the hon. member and reply in writing to the remaining questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: I will be happy to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad of the opportunity to take part in this debate, which is necessarily a brief one. I, too, heard what Dr. Lloyd Barber said as reported on CBC radio this morning. As Indian land claims commissioner, I assume he is not given to alarmist statements on this subject and knows what he is talking about. I was startled, and I think the people of Canada should be started, by his statement that the situation constituted an emergency. I am still not sure whether the department as a whole recognizes the gravity of the emergency.
He also spoke of the urgent necessity for a just, generous and fairly rapid settlement of Indian land claims. He spoke of the fact that if frustration continues as a result of the failure of the negotiations and discussions being held on Indian land claims, then we in Canada might find ourselves in a position similar to that in northern Ireland. I think we should take these warnings very, very seriously.
I wanted to call to the attention not only of the committee but of Canadians generally, a report that was made on

Canada's Indians by a minority rights group, a very prestigious group of jurists, scholars and others, I think mostly in the United Kingdom though also in Europe and other areas. They carried out a thorough study and a report was prepared quite recently by James Wilson. I want to thank the minister for sending me a copy of the report, which I read and found extremely interesting. I think it constitutes as good a summary of the background of this situation as any I have read. Naturally, it does not deal with all the complex details, but I hope Canadians will read it and understand it. If they do it will contribute to a change in attitude that seems to be essential to the finding of a solution.
This report was referred to in the House by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands during the debate on the Speech from the Throne, and I think it will become common knowledge. The report offers a fairly objective view of the Canadian scene and historical background. I do not have time to go into the report in detail, but there are one or two quotations I should like to make, First, the report begins:
After a century of spiritual and physical isolation, during which time they were commonly considered a dying race, the Canadian Indians have recently begun to emerge from the shadows and claim attention for their chronic problems of poverty, neglect and cultural and social alienation.
The report continues:
-the harsh facts of a poor and demoralized existence remain stubbornly unchanged for a majority of Canada's native people.
The report states that in spite of the complex efforts that have been made, the harsh facts remain the same. I see it is one o'clock, and I think I will have another five minutes or so when I have finished my hamburger.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ENSURE ADEQUATE INSPECTION OF MEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my statement will be very short and it will be essentially a summary of the statements I have made this week in answer to questions asked in this House by hon. members. Contrary to allegations made in the House this morning that I misled the House, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) will realize that what I am about to say is for the most part what I have already said in this House.
In view of the current concerns expressed over the quality of meat products, I know that many consumers are alarmed and I thought it would be appropriate to take a short period of the time of the House to make a summary of the situation in this regard. As a matter of fact, as I said a few minutes ago to the hon. member for St. John's East, I am surprised he needed 3*/2 hours to read a two-page document, most of which covered points that have already been covered this week.
The recent CBC program "Market Place" reported on studies carried out at the University of Guelph. The program implied that most of the samples tested were not safe for human consumption. The present programs and activities of my department do not substantiate this. As I said in this House on Wednesday, there are at present no epidemiological data to associate ground meat with human illness in Canada. My department has not received a single report from a doctor or a hospital relating human illness to the consumption of ground meat.
In the regular surveys carried out by the government's health protection branch, tests were negative for the organism salmonella which would have posed a health hazard. In both our survey and the work recently carried out at Guelph, with some assistance from my department I might add, this organism was absent. The total bacteriological count reported by "Market Place" is not related to a health hazard since these organisms do not produce toxins and are very readily destroyed by cooking. The high total count of bacteria reported in the program does suggest, however, that inadequate storage conditions with regard to time and temperature, and possibly unsanitary handling, may have occurred.
Like all members of this House, I want the best quality of food possible for Canadians.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ENSURE ADEQUATE INSPECTION OF MEAT
speechtext: That's a good idea.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ENSURE ADEQUATE INSPECTION OF MEAT
speechtext:
To this end, the health protection branch is doing the following. As I said in this House yesterday, regulations governing the protein quality and content of meat products and meat substitutes have been discussed with the food industry, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs over the last few months. These regulations are being forwarded to the Department of Justice for promulgation within the very near future.
Ground Beef
The second aspect of my department's regular work includes spot-checking samples of all meats across the country. In the most recent survey, 100 samples from 50 outlets were examined in five regions of the country. We found a total bacterial count lower than that reported on the "Market Place" program. As with any independent report of this nature, we will be checking their data, and if further action is warranted hon. members may be assured we will take it.
Several months ago the health protection branch planned a workshop for November 4 to November 6, 1974, for personnel involved in food control at the federal, provincial and municipal levels. Ground meat will be one of the topics of these discussions. As I said in this House last Wednesday, a new laboratory of the health protection branch on the campus of Saint Mary's University in Halifax will be opening on November 1 and will have a staff of 22 people working in microbiology on programs associated with the quality of foods. These personnel will be augmented by the necessary field staff in the regions to support our monitoring program, for which the total staff involvement will therefore be 30 persons in Halifax.
In view of the recent concern, I have instructed officials of my department to expand their program on microbiological standards for meats. In total, there are 245 people assigned to food programs in the field operations directorate of the branch. We will immediately assign 30 of our technical and professional staff in the field to work exclusively on meat samples across the country. This, of course, as I said this morning in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for St. John's East, will be in addition to the work normally being carried out by the 1,255 meat inspectors in the Department of Agriculture and by the 195 inspectors of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs involved in various aspects of food inspection.
It should also be noted that provincial and municipal governments are involved in food inspection. For provinces alone, for instance, there are over 1,500 inspectors associated with food programs across this country. The analyses that will come from the services to be carried out will help us to establish baseline levels of micro-organisms in meat on the Canadian market. From these results we will develop guidelines for use by the health protection branch and guidelines for provincial and municipal agencies in improving the sanitary aspects of meat processing. From this base, future regulatory programs will be developed. If substantiated cases of health hazards associated with ground meat are discovered, we shall not hesitate to take legal or regulatory action.
As I said in the House this morning, Canada has a food inspection program which compares favourably with that of any country in the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ENSURE ADEQUATE INSPECTION OF MEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say that the minister's statement, with all its shortcomings, would have saved us all a great deal of trouble had it been made last Monday. At least he would have been expressing his concern, instead of giving us the flippant and irresponsible answers we have experienced during the past week. Now we are being told there is no need to worry about bacteria and waste organisms in meat products. Indeed, typhoid and hepatitis, diseases which result from eating unclean food, are things of the past. However, in reality the decline of these diseases can only be attributed to the work of previous ministers of health who recognized the dire implications of the presence of bacteria in food and who enforced the regulations.
The physical symptoms which result from consuming food with a high bacterial content can range from mild diarrhoea to violent stomach upset. The absence of reported incidents in no way implies that sickness caused by poisonous ground beef does not exist. It may well be the case that these symptoms were attributed to some other cause. Does the minister prefer to wait until there is evidence of this type before taking action? Does somebody have to become seriously ill, as happened in the case of electric kettles and the lead poisoning which was uncovered by a very attentive nurse in Toronto who diagnosed lead poisoning contracted by a baby? Does the minister dispute the findings of the University of Guelph, that their samples contained human and animal waste; and does he not regard the existence of this foreign matter as constituting a health hazard? Would the minister serve meat infected by this kind of bacteria to his own children?
It is not uncommon for Canadians to prefer to eat their meat rare or in slightly cooked form. Does the minister feel that these people should change their eating habits because his department is incapable of instituting and enforcing regulations which would protect them from a potential health hazard? The minister told us that a high bacterial count could result from inadequate storage facilities. But he did not say what he intended to do about it. What steps does he intend to take to improve storage conditions at the supermarket level?
On Wednesday, the minister said the presence of coli bacteria does not constitute a health hazard if the meat is well cooked. He further stated that cooking at 160 degrees Fahrenheit would kill the bacteria. In other words, the secret is in the cooking. Now we are told, in a Canadian Press dispatch written after checking with an Ottawa hospital, that meat would have to be cooked for at least an hour at 172 degrees Fahrenheit to kill staph bacteria. Mr. Speaker, not even the minister would eat hamburger which had been cooked for an hour. He couldn't eat it; it would be too tough. Moreover, the Canadian Medical Association, according to the same dispatch, said to day that even cooking the meat at these higher temperatures would not necessarily ensure that all the bacteria were destroyed.
I know the minister would not want to mislead the House on a matter of such importance. We can only con-

elude, Mr. Speaker, that he is getting bad advice. The hon. gentleman has told us how much he has grown to like powdered milk. This was in response to our concern over the removal of the 5 per cent subsidy and the effect it would have upon the health of the country. He even went so far as to tell us that powdered milk improved if, after mixing, it was left in the refrigerator overnight. But hamburger cooked for an hour is stretching even the minister's credibility.
On Monday, when the subject was first raised in the House following the release by the CBC of the University of Guelph studies, the minister, instead of taking his responsibilities seriously and making a statement at the first opportunity, replied in a flippant and irresponsible manner. As a result of this flippancy and arrogance he now finds himself in hot water. This question, affecting as it does the health of Canadians, should have been treated by the minister as a matter of the utmost urgency and importance.
Now we turn to the presentation by the Food Prices Review Board. We saw the spectacle of the chairman of that board having to call a press conference to remind the Canadian public that the government was dragging its feet on the recommendations contained in the board's report on ground beef which has been in the hands of the government and, presumably, of the minister, since June 6. Lest anyone should doubt that, the chairman of the Food Prices Review Board made a formal statement. The response from the minister's department was that there were higher priorities within the department. That, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, was a most irresponsible reply. This is a most urgent matter and it directly affects Canadians because we are consuming more than 400 million pounds of ground beef. As a result of inflation the price of other cuts has risen beyond the reach of most Canadians.

The minister's statement today is not enough, when so many Canadians are concerned; and I suggest the reason for their concern is the irresponsible and flippant response given by the minister when he told us that coli bacteria are harmless if we cook our meat well.
We are now told we will have 30 inspectors seconded from other areas of responsibility. For how long? Is this to be temporary, or is it to be a permanent, new feature of the health inspection branch of the minister's department? I suggest that the time has come when we must change the regulations. We may even have to change the law. We may have to come up with stiffer penalties. We may even have to change the minister.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ENSURE ADEQUATE INSPECTION OF MEAT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my comments I should like to pay public tribute to two institutions in Canada which have done an excellent job in bringing this serious matter to the attention of the public and contributing in some way to getting the minister to act. I refer, first, to the CBC who did a good job of coverage in raising an important issue on a political program. It was responsible journalism of the finest kind. I refer, also, to the good work done in this respect by the Food Prices Review Board. It is good to see some public agencies performing well.
I turn now to another public agency, namely, the minister's department. I want to refer to a number of important omissions in the minister's statement. First, it is worth noting that for the first time, if one can find it in a statement a page and a half long, the minister actually says there is something wrong with our meat inspection procedures. He says there are some real hazards in this area and therefore he has taken steps to bring in new regulations and to increase the number of inspectors. At least, he has started to act and has acknowledged that a potentially dangerous situation exists. But what is missing? I would like to know when these important new regulations will be brought in. The minister did not give us a date, but he did acknowledge that he is finally going to move in that regard, and I hope it will be soon.
What about the action that the government will take if someone is found to be derelict in his responsibilities? What if it is discovered that people who keep the meat are not meeting the regulations laid down by his department? Are we going simply to have the maximum $50 fine, which I understand is the highest fine ever imposed upon someone who has not complied with the regulations? There is nothing in the minister's statement to say that the punitive aspect, in dealing with this situation, is to be considered. Surely that is a crucial matter, given the price of meat in Canada today. If you are caught neglecting your legal responsibilities, $50 is a negligible amount-perhaps
Ground Beef
only a very small part of an afternoon's sales in a store. Surely this is an inadequate fine for such a potentially serious offence.
The minister said there will be 30 full-time meat inspectors. My understanding-and the minister might clarify this-from the information we have been able to get, is that at least the equivalent of ten inspectors are working full time now, so we have an increase, presumably, of 20. I would like to know what the minister's criterion is. He has not said why we are going to have 30 inspectors now, as opposed to 50 or 500 or 1,500. Was it just guesswork? Was he simply saying, "Well, people are legitimately upset about this matter. We had better move in some direction. Let's increase it to 30"? Or was some rational criterion applied?
The minister did not indicate-and I think he should do so-why he thinks 30 is a reasonable number. Some people might think that 30 is a reasonable number for one city alone. I do not know the answer to that question; I will be candid about it. It might be a reasonable figure. But the minister, surely, has an obligation to say how the number was determined and to assure us that it was not simply a political response in the House of Commons to a critical situation.
There is another point I wish to make. It has a direct bearing on the number of inspectors who are now being put to work, but more broadly it has a direct bearing on the entire health protection program of the minister's department. Meat may be just one example of a potentially dangerous situation in the health field. Therefore, a very important part of the minister's department is the health protection program., I notice, Mr. Speaker, that the budget for this program has been virtually frozen for the last few years, with a very slight fluctuation. If the minister checks the figures he will find there has been no significant variation in the number of dollars allocated to this program. Given the rate of inflation in recent years, this means that real spending in the health protection program of his department has gone down in the past few years.
Surely if we are to deal with medical matters in a serious way, it would make much more sense to spend a lot of money before people become sick-to avoid illness; to avoid problems-than to pay for doctors after medical problems occur. I cannot forgo the opportunity of saying to my Conservative friends who are always complaining about government spending that this, surely, is an area where there should be more government spending to ensure that the people of Canada are protected and to avoid medical expenses, even if we are putting it on a dollars and cents basis.
I conclude my observations on the minister's statement with this point. It seems to me that the minister has displayed a totally unacceptable air of complacency. This is why he has been criticized by the Food Prices Review Board, by the opposition parties and by others. It arose from the statement in which he told the people of Canada, "You can drink powdered milk, if the price of milk is too high." I say to the minister that that is unacceptable. It is unacceptable, not only coming from a minister but from any Canadian whose income happens to be not particularly high, to tell people, "Drink powdered milk". The second

October 25, 1974
Ground Beef
illustration of this, which I mentioned in the House the other day and the hon. member for St. John's East mentioned it today, is in saying to the people of Canada, "Well, cook your hamburger a long time and then you don't have to worry. If you cook it at 160 degrees, you don't have to worry about bacteria."
I say to the minister that we should not have bacteria in our meat at any significant level, and we should not have to cook it at 160 degrees for up to an hour. If the minister or anyone in Canada wants to eat hamburger raw, we should be able to do so with complete safety.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I hope this situation will shock that minister out of his state of complacency, because if there is one field where complacency should be totally inacceptable, it is that of the health and welfare of Canadians. We need a totally new approach to this problem.

Mr. Speaker, I shall indicate first of all that the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) certainly contradicts the one made by the Chairman of the Food Prices Review Board. Even if this board is concerned with reviewing food prices, I seriously feel that, to be effective, it must also supervise not only the application of the Weights and Measures Act, but also make sure that food products are of satisfactory quality. This is the reason for the position adopted by the Chairman of this board concerning ground meat.
Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied that producers are not to blame when consumers do not get good quality meat. Cattle producers do their utmost to deliver healthy animals. At the slaughterhouses, the inspectors do an excellent job of protecting consumers, and I suggest that this is an important stage of meat marketing.
I have often had the opportunity of visiting slaughterhouses and I can bear witness to the efficiency of their inspections. Still, I am not so sure that the ground meat sold in supermarkets is always of top quality. It may be the result of unsanitary handling as well as aging of the meat.
The minister has stated that 240 persons are employed on food programs in various areas. In the future, he said, 30 technicians and professionals will devote all their time, from sea to sea, sampling meats, this, naturally, in addition to the work normally performed by the 1,255 inspectors from the Department of Agriculture and 195 others from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs who are responsible for the various aspects of food inspection.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the large number of people who, right across the country, supervise the quality of the meat offered the consumer in commercial establishments, in addition to provincial and municipal inspectors, I cannot understand that with such an army out in the field some firms should still break the law, at the present time by taking the risk of offering consumers meat of dubious quality.
Mr. Speaker, we agree that there is nothing better than good meat. On the other hand, nothing is so hard to digest,

so harmful for one's health than bad meat, meat that even dogs would eat with little enjoyment.
I feel strongly that, in addition to the steps to be taken by the various departments to ensure quality meat to the consumer, we should see to it immediately that the producers get sufficient profits and income to enable them to live decently and to continue producing enough to meet the needs of the domestic market.
Otherwise, they would have to import meat from somewhere else, and then the consumers might be entitled to complain louder about meat's bad quality.
So it is a very serious problem, and I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), with the help of the Cabinet, will introduce measures likely to improve the situation.
In conclusion, I hope the minister will have the courage to deal severely when necessary with the big corporations which deal in meat and do not comply with the legislation and regulations, in the same way he will deal severely if necessary with smaller businesses.

my bisected remarks. I was referring to the report of the minority rights group regarding Canadian Indians. I read a few excerpts from the report because I find it particularly worth while and interesting. I should like to read further from page 7 of the report:
The simple fact is that successive governments have found it easier and cheaper to keep the Indians dependent on welfare than to make the enormous capital investment required to enable them to stand on their own feet.
The economic effects of this policy can be easily measured: unemployment among Canadians as a whole is 6 per cent, among Indians it is 50 per cent. In 1969 the average income of a Canadian family was $8,874; while 88 per cent of all Indian families made less than $3,000, and about 50 per cent made less than $1,000 .. . including all welfare payments.
I continue reading from the report:
Despite these encouraging signs there has still not been a major transformation of Indian life. The Department of Indian Affairs is still a huge and costly vested interest and may, wittingly or unwittingly, obstruct the movement of power and resources to the Indians ... There is a long history of failure, parsimony and neglect to be made up for.
I draw this matter to the minister's attention, not because he condones or wills that this should be so but because he should recognize how difficult is the task he has undertaken.
Finally, the document reads:
In order to make this more trusting atmosphere possible, and give the Indians the best chance of success in finding solutions to their chronic ills, the government will have to act in good faith and make available to them adequate resources for a long period of experiment and development, and Canadians as a whole must abdicate the responsibility they assumed for deciding whether "their" Indians should be "preserved" or assimilated. Whatever paths the Indians decide to follow, and however unwise they may appear to outsiders, the choice must now be made by the Indians themselves. White Canadians are not being asked to determine what the Indian was or is or could become; they are being asked to do something far more difficult; accept him as he is.
May I say a few words about property and land claims. This is a difficult and complex matter and I want to sound a note of warning. If it is dealt with in a purely legalistic manner, it will not succeed. It must be dealt with in a statesmanlike manner. These problems need political judgment and probably legislation. I wish to ask the minister some questions on this matter. He has told us of some of the negotiations and has expressed optimism about the negotiations relating to northern Quebec. I understand these are being conducted primarily with the Quebec government.
I ask about the other negotiations. How are they getting on. Are they progressing? Are adequate funds being made available to enable Indians to carry out adequate research for the presentation of their cases? I stress the need for adequate funds. Are they being made available? Is the process of negotiation being used with regard to aboriginal claims, and also respecting those who have had settlement of their treaty rights but claim that their treaty rights are being disregarded? This needs to be rectified because the treaties were totally unfair when first entered into.

Madam Chairman, the procedure in committee of the whole is somewhat strange to me. Nevertheless, I am pleased to have this opportunity to explain my views during the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I am interested in many aspects of the department, particularly the parks branch and the branch concerned with Indian affairs. Most of the national park known as Kouchibouguac is in my constituency. Actually, I share the honour with the Minister of State (Fisheries). A new national park, known as Beaubear's Island, is being constructed in my area because of the generosity of the late Lieutenant-Governor of New Brunswick, Hon. J. Leonard O'Brien, who donated the island to the people of Canada for that purpose.
Today I shall speak about education, particularly as it relates to the Indian people of Canada. I hope to see the day when the department will no longer be necessary and the Indian people of this nation will not look to departments of government but will rely on their own competence to accomplish their goals and attain their destinies. It is to be regretted that there is a so-called Indian problem today. If there is a problem, the responsibility cannot be laid at the feet of any one government but must be shared collectively by all governments and by all white people, as this process has gone on since the white man began colonizing this continent. On the day the first white man set foot on the shores of North America, the so-called Indian problem began. I am not sure that we cannot call it the white man's problem. I am sure the Indians would.
In the beginning, white men attempted to solve the problem by confronting the Indians. White men tried to make the Indian adopt the white man's culture. I will not quarrel with our ancestors, who I believe were sincere in their efforts. However, they were not completely successful. Some Indians resisted and the white man used his traditional method of solving problems, that is, the gun. For several generations we perpetuated the notion that we came here to convert savages but they resisted our efforts. Any battle with Indians which the white man won, was won by superior tactics and incredible bravery. On the other hand, if we lost to the Indians it was through treachery and sneak attacks and we subsequently set it down as a massacre. In my view, any battle is a massacre. However, the bias of the historian makes a great difference.
Fortunately, our attitude in recent years has changed. We want to see Indians take their rightful place in the fabric of society and of Canadian life. In the past half-dozen years the consultative process has begun to function to the benefit of the Indian people and the Canadian government. I hope that this consultative process will continue and will be enshrined in the spirit of departmental operations. I am sure the minister shares this view.
If the Indian people of Canada are to achieve their goals, it will be necessary for us to introduce improved educational programs. A very high proportion of Indian children drop out of school because the education they receive has no relevance to their lives. We need education which will help the Indian people meet their aims. It is not necessary that curriculums for Indian children should be the same as
those for whites. Such a program is not logical. Indian education should be designed around the traditional skills, culture and heritage of the Indian peoples because these are the skills they will find useful.
I do not think we should educate the native peoples of Canada in such a way that they will lose their heritage and culture. It is imperative that they acquire skills which will enable them to live independently and in keeping with the dignity which is so necessary to the nature of man. When Indians attend public schools because of arrangements with provincial departments of education, we must be particularly careful to make sure they retain their culture and heritage. In my limited experience of teaching Indian children, I have found they are not capable of coping with our system, because it is largely irrelevant to them. So when we force them to undergo our sort of education we are not keeping in tune with their interests.
I have seen parents take their children out of school to hunt caribou or look after trap lines. Some people have expressed despair that this should be so. Personally, I think this kind of activity can have significant educational value if the system is designed to fit this kind of learning experience into the over-all pattern of native education. That is not to suggest that we should keep our native people as hunters, fishermen and trappers. However, there is nothing wrong with that if it is what some of them want to do.
I want to state as firmly as I can that education of the native people must improve both quantitatively and qualitatively. I am confident the minister shares this view and will make every effort to ensure our native children the best possible educational opportunities. However, all our efforts to improve their education will go for naught unless employment opportunity is available and accompanies the improving educational opportunity which we provide. I look forward to the day when the native peoples of Canada will take their place alongside the rest of us in whatever walk of life they choose.

Madam Chairman, I shall deal with no more than two of the major problems in northern Manitoba, the area with which I am most familiar. However, I feel these two subjects affect the entire country. In the past three weeks we have heard a great deal about Indian and native housing. I admit it is a problem. I travelled with the minister into several parts of my constituency where we saw the situation at first-hand.
Housing in many parts of our reserves is one of the most needed commodities. However, we seem to have the idea that housing must be built to our standard. If the Indians do not accept the standard we have set for them, there just does not seem to be any housing available. Professors say that everyone must have so many feet of air space. Let me assure you, Madam Chairman, that the rate at which we are building houses on reserves today cannot keep up with the population explosion taking place on the reserves. I am sure all hon. members are aware of that fact.
My idea to eliminate some of the problems in housing is this. A certain percentage of houses should be built each
[The Assistant Deputy Chairman]
October 25, 1974

year on any given reserve. I am not sure how they are allocated. However, there are still many people on the reserves who would be very happy to have a roof over their heads. With the oncoming winter, we still face the problem of having two or three families living in one home. I wish to emphasize to the minister that there are ways in which we can accommodate people on the reserves. We can go right back to the old log home. In most cases the timber is in the area and the people are skilled in the construction of this type of home; they do not need training programs in order to build them. I am not talking about a 12 by 14 foot log home but about a home in which a family can survive.
The unemployment rate in my constituency is 12.8 per cent. We have LIP and a step, "A HOP" and a jump programs to do all kinds of things to create employment. These people in my constituency could be employed and housing could be provided for them at the same time. This is what is wanted by the people in many of the communities which I represent. They would be very happy to be able to move into a small home: let's call it a transitional type of home. The log home was the traditional until a few years ago when we stepped in and told the Indians they needed gyproc on the inside and something else on the outside. A good log home can be built by the people in the community at one third of the cost of today's traditional home.
The biggest problem facing people in the north is the high cost of transporting materials to the reserves. Half the money is used for that. I next want to speak about the alcohol problem which faces our Indian people. It is a problem which we, along with the Indian people, must overcome or the whole system will break down. Neither we nor the Indian people can cope with the alcohol problem. I am not a world traveller; I am only talking of my constituency. The chiefs and the people in my area admit there is a problem and they are trying to do something about it.
I cannot find in the estimates the amount of money which will help these people overcome this serious problem. Is it included in the $82 million set aside for professional help? Sending professional people to help them will not solve the problem. Someone comes in with a theory that if you all get together, hold hands and talk about the problem, it will go away. That theory should go out the window. The problem has to be dealt with by the people on the reserves. We can provide some expertise, but they must recognize that it is their problem. I would like to see an effort made to help them.
I understand that the community development program will be, or has been cut back to some extent. I do not believe I have been a strong promoter of community development programs, but I feel there must be a continuing program to help educate the people living on reserves.
This morning the minister referred to the transfer of funds to the band level. I support that idea. However, the necessary training must accompany this program. In many areas the native people want to have funds. There is no doubt about that. They should have them. However, they also need training so they do not end up with pie all over their faces. This is what has happened in many cases. Indian Affairs have been in too much of a rush to turn
Estimates
everything over to the band and let them go it on their own. Some of the bands have fallen down badly. Indian Affairs have been forced to return and take over these services because of the mess some bands made of it. That is why I want a community development program which will ensure that the bands are trained to carry on their own programs. They would then be much happier in handling their own programs.
The minister spoke this morning about utilizing reserves land, and so on. I am in favour of this. However, there is one problem in my constituency. At The Pas reserve a large complex is now being built. I admit that I am not up to date on everything that is happening there. However, I do not believe many of the people in the adjoining communities are in tune with just what is happening at that complex. There should be more communication between the adjoining town of The Pas and Indian Affairs so each can be apprised of where the other stands in this regard.
I say that because The Pas stands to lose a lot of tax money with a facility like this on the reserve. There should therefore be a little more consultation between Indian Affairs and the people of The Pas so as to let everyone know exactly where they stand.
Another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the committee is the alcohol problem. I am sure all hon. members are aware of the statistic that 85 per cent of the Indian people who fill our jails today have been convicted of alcohol offences. I should like to see the Department of Indian Affairs, through its educational programs, work very closely with the bands and help them overcome this very serious problem which is going to be the backbreaker of every reserve in northern Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, so I do not transgress upon the desire of several hon. members who wish to speak, all I shall say at this point is that I am very sympathetic to the remarks made by the hon. member. He dealt with several areas, and the first was the provision of log homes. As a youngster I spent some time in one in Athabasca, and one of the first things that I did when I came to this department was to look into that possibility.
As hon. members know, our most critical housing areas are northern Quebec and Ontario, across the northern part of the three prairie provinces into B.C. and down the Mackenzie valley, all areas where, as far as I and, it seems, as far as the hon. member is concerned, there is potential to build log homes. He is quite right in drawing that to our attention.

Madam Chairman, during the few minutes at my disposal, I should like to talk about the estimates for Parks Canada.
National parks contain characteristics of great beauty which are protected for the benefit of Canadians and future generations.
Canada is a young country where a large part of the population lived not so long ago in or near the wilderness.

Today, most Canadians are within easy reach of areas which are still suited for outdoor activities. However, Canadians do not care for these outdoor activities. They will have to learn from the experience of densely populated countries respecting the preservation and conservation of areas which can be converted into national parks.
As the population and urban development increase, it will be increasingly imperative to keep these areas in their natural state and it will cost more and more money. Madam Chairman, this brings me to call your attention to an article in yesterday's issue of La Presse to the effect that Kuwait is purchasing an American island with $17.4 million of its oil profits. Kuwait has just added to its territory a small island called Kiawah in the Atlantic, only 30 kilometers from Charleston, South Carolina.
The developer chosen by the Kuwaiti to convert this wooded island into a large and highly profitable amusement park believes that this purchase could be the first of a series of investments by Kuwait in American holiday spots. This small island, sold for $17.4 million, was bought in 1955 by an American promoter for $125,000. This week's transaction in South Carolina should make us think about preserving our historical sites, of our enchanting sites in Canada, so that they do not become foreign-owned.
Thus, Madam Chairman, it is important to recognize from now on the wilderness areas in Canada and to take them into account when putting forward a policy on the national parks purpose, and thus provide for the development of the system. Speaking of the development of the park system, I must pay tribute to the president of the Privy Council (Mr. Chretien) who established ten national parks in Canada between 1970 and 1974. I think this House should pay tribute to this great Canadian for his great concern for preservation.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Madam Chairman. Our understanding, and the understanding held by the House leaders, with respect to this particular series of estimates in committee of the whole was that this was going to be primarily a committee hearing for the use of the opposition, to enable them to examine ministers on the government spending estimates for the year 1974-75. As a result of that understanding, and in view of the importance of these three days, we agreed with this procedure.
In the House this afternoon we have, for some reason or other, government members rising in their places; there was one over there a few minutes ago and now we have my hon. friend. They have been making speeches that laud ministers. This is not the purpose of the committee of the whole on estimates, and I must protest. I do so reluctantly, Madam Chairman, but I must protest. If this is allowed to continue-I say this with great respect-through the rest of the afternoon, then we are destroying what is a very important experiment in parliamentary procedure, this operation upon which we are engaged.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I do not want in any way to detract from my colleagues' right to speak. But I would ask you, Madam Chairman, and my hon. friends on the other side of the House to remember

the understanding reached between the government House leader, the opposition House leader and, as I understand it, the House leader for the New Democratic Party. If government members continue to pay homage to ministers-we know they all pay homage to their own-then we are destroying the purpose of this experiment, which frankly we think is a very valuable one in the course of the reform of parliament that the Prime Minister himself mentioned. I say this with respect, but in the circumstances I felt I could not sit here any longer and not say anything.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: On the same point of order, Madam Chairman, I do not think it is possible for members on this side of the House to accept the principle that the House of Commons belongs to members of the opposition.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The agreement reached between the House leaders was that we would revert to the old system of committee of supply as an experiment. That we have done. In committee of supply in my time in the House of Commons-before the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton came here-government members used to speak in the same way as opposition members, and this has been going on today. There are members on this side who represent large numbers of Indians and who have not spoken; I am one of them. There are a large number who would like to speak. My point of order is that, to my knowledge, there was no agreement that Liberal members would not participate in debate; and I reject wholly the proposition that the House of Commons belongs only to members of the opposition.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, the parliamentary secretary is quite right if he says there is no House order in that regard. The government House leader indicated that perhaps it might become inflexible if there were a House order, and I agree with him. Nonetheless, there was an understanding that, because of the experimental nature of this, and the circumstances under which this agreement was reached, government members would not over-extend their time.
Right now we are standing at a point with three speakers from the government side and we have had three speakers from the opposition side. I think the undertaking and the understanding have now been breached, and I continue my protest with regard to the understanding that was reached. Since we are trying an experiment in the course of the consideration of these estimates I think things are being badly affected by the attitude of the government, and by the parliamentary secretary who spoke for the government on this matter.
On a point of order, Madam Chairman.
