On Schedule A-Department of Public Works [Translation]

Madam Chairman, I should like to avail myself of the opportunity of this debate on the estimates of the Department of Public Works to make certain representations to the Minister on the urgent needs of the area in connection with wharves and channels.
Even if a member is elected to represent the Canadian people as a whole, he must nevertheless have a greater concern for the problems of his constituency.
As far as the ministers are concerned, namely the executive members, I suggest they must administer the funds entrusted to them by Parliament so that every area of this country gets its fair share. Therefore, I wish to call the attention of the minister on very important matters that concern all the South Shore people, namely Montmagny and its suburban area. In the 1974-75 estimates, one can see that the department's objectives concerning the marine program is to provide and maintain at the most economical cost marine facilities as required by federal programs for the development and support of industry and for water level control. Secondly, this program provides for the construction, improvement and maintenance of marine structures, the planning and establishment of channels, wharves and harbours to facilitate the transportation of passengers and bulk and general cargo. That is a very clear objective.
For a number of years, representations have been made to the federal government by the municipal authorities of the city of Montmagny, middle officials and people in general through petitions to have dredging operations carried out in the channel leading to the wharf in Montmagny, but so far in vain.
All members who have represented that area in Parliament made representations to the various levels of government. Liberal and Conservative members, and even the

October 25, 1974
Estimates
Hon. Jean Lesage, when he was the hon. member for Montmagny-l'Islet, made representations to that effect. Whether the governments were Liberal or Conservative, the answer was always no. I do not think that the authorities were motivated by partisanship in their refusal. However, there is an extensive record on the channel to Mont-magny, It is not because the various ministers who were in charge of the department of Public Works and the department of Transport are unaware of the unfavourable situation of Montmagny that the problem has remained unsolved. On the contrary, the problem is quite clear to them. However, I think more and more that it is the bureaucracy that ill-advises the ministers and tells them that the nature of the work to be done would be extremely expensive and would not be viable. In support of that I will quote a paragraph of the letter from the director of the Quebec district:
The answers boil down to that: the department agrees that this project could improve the tourist industry and promote trade traffic. However, quayage revenues would not warrant the cost of the improvements which would reach over half a million dollars and for those reasons, the department would not be justified in authorizing that project.
That is one version, but there are others. Looking very closely at that record, one can realize that the various civil servants who studied the matter do not agree about costs. Some speak in terms of $500,000 and others in terms of $750,000. I have come to the conclusion that if we really wish to contribute to the development of the South Shore area, we should not hesitate to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to do the necessary works and to exploit those vast touristic resources which are natural but which need man's intervention to become profitable. Furthermore, it would create many jobs. If we were ready to spend one tenth of the money wasted on the refitting of the Bonaventure, all the people of the South Shore would be very proud of it and this would make us forget the unfortunate case of the Bonaventure.
In Montmagny and the vicinity, there are many islands, especially l'lle aux Grues, opposite Montmagny, that is inhabited by many brave people eager to develop this island further and who would wish to go on living there, but with means of communication which would be adequate in 1974. The transportation system available to them is inadequate. It would be necessary to make major improvements to the island dock, and I ask the minister to take note of that so that an amount be provided for that purpose in the next estimates of 1975-76.
I spoke some time ago of the benefits that the dredging of the channel would bring to the South Shore.
But there would also be many advantages for the islands because the tourists would find access much easier.
The government calls on local initiatives to stimulate our economy. That is all well and good. But I think we should make more use of the natural advantages to be found in our area. One of them is the tourist industry with all the developments it can bring in this area.
For several years, a lot has been said about industrial decentralization. I, for one, suggest that decentralization is urgent but talking is not enough: action must follow and the faster the better.
Dragging the channel and repairing the Montmagny wharf would greatly help the region. In my opinion Mont-

magny is the capital of the south shore. If industry is to be attracted a centre of attraction must be created and to do this the co-operation of government authorities at all levels is needed. And as the federal government swells its offers with the greater part of what the taxpayers must part with it is normal that the federal government should be responsible for the work of dragging the channel and repairing the wharf.
May I be allowed, Madam Chairman, to take this opportunity to thank the ex-minister of public works, the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Dube), for having accepted to put on the 1975-76 program an amount of $14 million towards the rebuilding of the Montmagny wharf. I am asking the new minister to consider continuing his predecessor's program and I am confident of the minister's understanding and I congratulate him on his new post. I am also asking the minister to take into account the representations made to his department by the authorities of the city of Montmagny concerning the damages done each year by the spring break-up on the South River, near the Rivard bridge, in Montmagny. To prevent a recurrence of these damages, it would be absolutely necessary that a wall be built from the Rivard bridge towards the falls to eliminate the right angle which is the main cause of the damages suffered.
I also take this opportunity to ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury) to review legislation and regulations dealing with retaining walls along the St. Lawrence River. It is regrettable that retaining walls built some years ago are now in a deplorable state because they are not regularly repaired. They are in particularly bad shape along the coast opposite the Saint-Michel-de-Bellechasse municipality in Montmagny. The municipal authorities have often made representations for restoration or repairs to these retaining walls, but department employees always found the right answer to free themselves from that responsibility. Nevertheless, if the department feels that it must allocate too much money for maintenance, may we seriously-

I have never understood that there was an agreement on the votes of the department. There was an agreement on the others but not on this one, and I do not think I abused the time of the House this week on the votes; I would like to take a couple of minutes to conclude my speech.

Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will bear in mind the representations I just made, and will find a way out of the embankment walls' lack of maintenance as soon as possible, so that the existing walls at least can be kept up.
I would also request the up-grading of the breakwater of the community of Berthier-sur-mer, which used to be called Berthier-en-Bas. In 1970, the department spent several thousands of dollars for repairs on that breakwater, which is of very great historical value. I know that won't earn people a living, but they value it a lot! I do think it is worth being maintained. That breakwater has been entered lately as a ruin on marine charts. I feel sorry about that. The hon. member for Bellechasse, who lives in Berthier-sur-Mer, deserves no credit for it. Moreover, the waters are quite deep in that area, and if the breakwater was upgraded, it could be put to a very practical use.
There is more and more talk about a Canadian merchant navy. If it becomes a reality some day, and the sooner the better, we shall be glad then to use that wharf. Finally, I thank the Minister for the upgrading work under way at the Montmagny federal building. I am sure the people will welcome it, and the civil servants who work in that building will feel more at ease and, consequently, will be more efficient in their work.
Those, Mr. Chairman, were the remarks I wanted to make on the occasion of the examination of these estimates. In the name of the South Shore people, I hope the Minister will see those representations in a favourable eye so that jobs be created in our area which experiences an unemployment rate of 11.3 per cent and so that our skilled workers be put to a better use for everyone's well being and in order to fight inflation efficiently.

Mr. Chairman, I am delighted to have the opportunity to participate in the discussion on the estimates this afternoon. Recently I spent a fair length of time on the same subject in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. I join many members on this side of the House who claim that we do not have enough time to scrutinize the accounts.
A Public Works project was before the standing committee for only one meeting. Given the usual delays, that meant we had only eighty minutes. Given the make up of the committee, this meant that my colleague and I had only a total of 28 minutes in which to examine the estimates of $522,747,000. If you break that down, approval had to come at approximately $315,000 per second.
It is bad enough that these huge amounts have to be considered with lightning speed, but the one man responsible for this budget, the Minister of Public Works, felt it was beneath him and did not bother to show up at the meeting at all. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River had the audacity on Wednesday to stand up in the House and lecture us, with his arrogant and insolent finger waving in the air, telling us that a careful examination of the estimates was needed. Of all the unmitigated gall!
Estimates
Not only did he utter the most senseless drivel I have ever heard, but he did it from the Prime Minister's chair. He must have been swept away by delusions of grandeur. The minister did send along his deputy to the committee meeting together with his staff who, I guess, all told probably collect a few thousand dollars an hour. The deputy minister, Mr. MacDonald, is a very competent fellow. I found him to be knowledgeable and willing to co-operate. His answers sometimes contained that loquacious multisyllabic nomenclature typical of all senior civil servants.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Say that again.

I am sure I can say it better the second time than I did the first. On the whole, he is an excellent administrator. However, I am sure he would be the first to admit that the responsibility must lie with the minister who has been elected and is responsible to this House. Nevertheless, the minister felt it was beneath him to attend the meeting. Perhaps he will understand that I am delighted to be here to put some questions on the record. I say "on the record" because I will put my questions in a list, and frankly I want the minister to answer them, but I expect I will run out of time. Perhaps he will have a chance to answer them later.
Coupled with the unwillingness of the minister to attend the meeting and be questioned is the matter of the annual report of the Public Works Department, which is usually the basis for a good deal of questioning. Although the minister may have inserted the document in the record somewhere, it was described by the deputy minister as an advance copy on October 15, and I, did not see the document publicly placed on the record after that date. In fact the report must have been around for quite some time since it was over the signature of the former minister, the hon. member for Restigouche. Many of my questions will relate to that report.
But first I must question the sanity of a department which, even in these inflationary times, allows its budget to gallop along at the rate of 38 per cent in two years, from $375 million in 1972-73 to $520 million in 1974-75. Is it any wonder we have inflation? Can there be any question of who is feeding the most fuel on the fires of inflation? Some of the questions which I wish to put forward have to do with some comparisons that I have made.
In the annual report estimates, Place Guy Favreau in Montreal, Quebec, is shown at $173 million. The estimated total cost, however, in the 1973-74 estimates is shown at only $87 million. The previously estimated total cost was only $42 million. Is this building now going to cost four times what it was supposed to cost originally?
Also in Montreal is the M.A.P.P. building, which shows in the annual report at $184 million. It is placed in the estimates at which we are looking right now, at $53 million, and before that, for some unknown reason, a year earlier it was $3 million more, or $56 million. Again, is that building going to cost us three and a half times the price at which it was estimated originally?
There is a small building in Ottawa at which I look with real concern, namely, the building for the Department of Urban Affairs, the former LaSalle Academy. The annual report estimates it at $7 million. The estimates that we are given show it at only $5 million, and a year ago it was

October 25, 1974
Estimates
estimated at only $4.3 million. I strongly suspect this will be extremely expensive housing for the Minister of State for Urban Affairs.
The Toronto, Ontario, M.A.P.P. building presents an even stranger picture. The annual report estimates show it at $140 million. The estimate before us today shows it at $121 million, but the previous estimate shows it at $200 million. The previous year that same building was estimated at $80 million. From $80 million to $200 million, down to $121 million, and then back up to $140 million- surely someone must have a reasonable idea what this building will cost, but obviously it is not the Department of Public Works.
We do not have to restrict ourselves to these large buildings. We could consider a small government of Canada building in Nova Scotia which, two years ago, was estimated at $850,000. No'-' it is up to $2.4 million. Again there is one million dollars difference in what the estimates show. In Calgary, Alberta, we have a government of Canada building estimated at $25 million in the annual report. The previous estimates show it at only $18.5 million. There is one other government of Canada building on Sparks Street in Ottawa that is now listed at $56 million in the annual report. It is only $49 million in the estimates before us, and in last year's estimates it was to be only $36.7 million.
If we take those seven buildings we find that the difference between the estimates that we are asked to scrutinize and the estimates that are in the annual report vary by a total of $251.6 million. How are we supposed to make a reasonable scrutiny of two documents put out by the same department, supposedly at the same time, with a discrepancy of a quarter of a billion dollars? We cannot possibly come up with reasonable and sensible answers if this is the case.
I took a look at some of the other discrepancies. I was interested because members of parliament receive other documents besides the estimates. We also receive the Public Accounts books, and I thought it might be interesting to look at them to see what they had to say about some of the estimates. For example, we find at Acton Vale, which is somewhere in Quebec-I do not even know where-a little government of Canada building there for which there is a tender for $316,000. That may be a reasonable amount for that building; I do not know. The estimates say it was going to be $338,000. So, for a change, it appears to be within the budget.
The estimates for 1973-74 say $338,000, but the Public Accounts books say that a contract was let for $324,000, or a difference of $8,000. In addition, the Public Accounts estimate for 1973-74 was only $228,000. Public Accounts do not dream up these figures, they must get them from somewhere. I suggest they come from the department. If the department gives Public Accounts an estimate of $228,000 on the one hand and puts before the House of Commons a figure of $338,000 in the annual estimates, obviously something is wrong.
I am going to take a few more minutes to go through similar examples. At Beloeil, Quebec, a government of Canada building was shown, finally, at $599,900. That sounds like a good deal, but the estimates for 1974-75

showed $652,000, and the estimates for 1973-74 showed $814,000. While some of us might be accused of being gullible we do not believe that this building can have depreciated by 25 per cent while everything else has gone up in cost. So, I looked back at the Public Accounts estimate and found that their report for 1973-74 was $350,000. I wonder where Public Accounts got that estimate. If the Department of Public Works is giving out two sets of figures I should like to know why.
In Stouffville, Ontario, there is a little post office at $257,800 with the estimates showing previously at $342,000 and $325,000, while Public Accounts show $195,000. These figures vary too much for us to take reasonable cognizance of them, Mr. Chairman, yet we are told by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council that we have enough time to scrutinize them in committee.
There is one last thing that I want to bring to the attention of the committee. Assuming that the estimates given to us by the department are valid, let me just report four items that I have picked out across Canada.
The estimates show a renovation in Arvida, Quebec, at $281,000; the contract was let at $340,000, a considerable difference. In Downsview, Ontario, for a postal station the estimates show $290,000; the contract was $348,000. In St. John's, Newfoundland, another mail processing facility, the estimate was $3,700,000, and the actual contract $6,199,000. In Terrebonne, Quebec the estimates show $293,000, and the actual contract $343,000.
If this level of inflationary spending is to continue, I should like to know if the department is going ahead erecting every building it has on its drawing boards and inflating its budget completely out of reason. Would it not be better to slow down and look at government spending?
While I do not want to offend my friends in Alberta, nevertheless I find that a building is shown in Lethbridge, Alberta, for $22,159,885 and the contract let. I looked diligently but I could not find it anywhere in the estimates. I do not know where that one sprang from, Mr. Chairman. Somehow we dreamed up a building very quickly, but I could not find it in either book.
I merely want to say in closing that we have little enough time to scrutinize these estimates. The figures are stunning in size and complexity, and I think it is high time we had a different method of presenting them, and certainly a different method of studying them.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to abuse my privilege, but I would merely like to make a remark. I regret that, when we make claims for some retaining walls which were built a few years ago with the use of gabions- cylinders of wicker filled with stones-those gabions have completely deteriorated after decades and then we get to the department whose budget we are studying to find out that there is no money to provide for the maintenance and repair of those walls.
I think that if the government had retaining walls built, it is because they thought it was necessary to protect the banks, and it must act as any citizen would and provide for the upkeep of the property. And if it is left to individuals it would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that the Canadian
October 25, 1974

government should at least help them provide for the maintenance of those walls.
In the riding of Portneuf, Mr. Chairman, this problem is frequent and we are told there are no funds. I would like the Minister of Public Works to provide funds, at least to maintain the retaining walls already built in several places in the riding of Portneuf.
Mr. Chairman, I would also point out a certain lack of coherence which now and again becomes apparent in administrative decisions. In Cap-Sante, for example, also in the same electoral district, a boat landing has been built near the wharf. Unfortunately, there is no road from Cap-Sante to this wharf. Money has been invested for a boat landing but there is no road. If we ask for one, we are told there is no fund to solve this problem.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I will now leave the floor to the next speaker.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few questions for the minister. In the Department of Public Works annual report for the fiscal year April 1, 1973, to March 31, 1974, there is reference to the Enoch Indian Band Development Study. On October 22, 1973, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development invited the Department of Public Works property development branch to prepare a detailed feasibility study on the development of a native planned community for up to 40,000 people on the Enoch Indian reservation at Winterburn, Alberta.
This land was surrendered by the band for the purpose of generating revenues from leasehold developments. Indian Affairs set aside payment fees and expenses of $120,000. Has the Department of Public Works put any money into this project and, if so, how much?

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question on behalf of a colleague who cannot be here. I understand that in the community of White Rock there is a breakwater type of harbour which is in serious disrepair. Does the Department of Public Works intend to bring that dock up to standard? Apparently it is dangerous right now. I gather there was some move to turn the facility over to the community, but the community cannot afford it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my answer will also interest the hon. member for Bellechasse. The development and, to some degree, maintenance of harbours, falls under two jurisdictions. Harbours devoted primarily to commercial purposes are the developmental responsibility of the Department of Transport, which determines priorities in this area and commissions the Department of Public Works to execute the necessary works.
With regard to fishing and pleasure or tourist harbours and marinas, development is the responsibility of the Department of the Environment. Funds available to the Department of the Environment are devoted to priorities established by that department. Again, the Department of Public Works is commissioned by either of those two departments to carry out the actual work. The Department of Public Works is responsible for the provision of technical advice. The responsibility for determining whether the work is to be carried out belongs either to the Minister of Transport or the Minister of the Environment.
Are projects carried out by the Department of Public Works on the basis of merit, or is there a formula under which the department allocates projects in accordance with some regional plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the same question was asked in the standing committee, and the answer furnished by the deputy minister was substantially the same as the one I shall give. There is neither a cast iron nor rigid formula in the examination of any particular project. It is, however, looked at within a general framework. A variety of considerations have to be taken into account. Those considerations will vary with each project.

Mr. Chairman, some years ago, where retaining walls were concerned, the practice was that the Public Works Department was paying the cost when the channel was running within 2,000 feet of the shore line and if it was between 2,000 and 3,000 feet from it they paid 50 per cent of the cost and if it was 3,000 feet or more away from the shore, they paid one third of the cost.
I was surprised when after my election I came upon several reports on that subject. In my riding, many lots lie within 1,500 feet from the shore. I considered that problem with the officials of the department and the municipal authorities and yet there are no sustaining walls. The final answer that I received from the department was that they had not provided money in their budget for that purpose. I wonder if there is a policy on land ownership. Also they could have established a policy on the access to ownership. Maybe they could have also established a policy with respect to conservation of personal properties.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the question of sustaining walls is very interesting. Many years ago, a formula was devised concerning what we call water lots. There is also an alternative technique for retaining the ground. It seems that the method used in the water where water lots are concerned did not require any change while the method relating to ground is under current review. That is what I could answer now to the hon. member.
